reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Shields' Textbook of Glaucoma
clinicalPearls: A benign, non-infective inflammatory process of the orbit with no identifiable local or systemic cause, and a diagnosis reached largely by exclusion
It classically presents with acute, painful proptosis, periorbital swelling and redness, chemosis, and restricted eye movements with diplopia
Any orbital structure may be involved, giving subtypes such as myositic, lacrimal (dacryoadenitis), anterior, apical, and diffuse patterns
Involvement of the orbital apex can threaten vision through optic-nerve compression
Imaging shows inflammatory infiltration that may involve muscles including their tendons, the lacrimal gland, or diffuse orbital fat, without a discrete mass
A characteristically rapid and dramatic response to systemic corticosteroids supports the diagnosis, though relapse on withdrawal is common
Atypical, bilateral, recurrent, or steroid-unresponsive cases require biopsy and workup to exclude lymphoma, specific inflammations, and IgG4-related disease
It is distinguished from thyroid eye disease, which is usually less painful and spares muscle tendons, and from orbital cellulitis, which is infective
reference.pathophysiology: Idiopathic orbital inflammation is a polymorphous inflammatory infiltrate of orbital tissues, comprising lymphocytes, plasma cells, and variable fibrosis, that occurs without an identifiable infective, neoplastic, or systemic autoimmune cause. The inflammation may target any orbital component, producing the myositic, dacryoadenitis, anterior, apical, or diffuse patterns, and the resulting swelling and mass effect cause pain, proptosis, congestion, and restriction of eye movement. Some cases represent part of the IgG4-related disease spectrum. The condition is thought to be immune-mediated, which underlies its responsiveness to corticosteroids, but the tendency to relapse and to develop fibrosis reflects an ongoing dysregulated inflammatory drive.
additionalDifferentials: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other systemic vasculitides
additionalInvestigations: Orbital CT or MRI to define the pattern and extent of inflammation and exclude a discrete mass
Assessment of visual acuity, colour vision, and pupils to detect optic-nerve involvement
Bloods including inflammatory markers, and serum IgG4, with ANCA and thyroid function to exclude mimics
Orbital biopsy in atypical, recurrent, bilateral, or steroid-unresponsive disease
Systemic evaluation for sarcoidosis, vasculitis, or lymphoproliferative disease when indicated
Monitoring of response and relapse during and after corticosteroid treatment
redFlags: Reduced acuity or colour vision suggesting apical optic-nerve compression
Failure to respond promptly to corticosteroids, raising suspicion of lymphoma or specific inflammation
Bilateral or recurrent disease pointing to a systemic or IgG4-related cause
Rapidly progressive proptosis with severe pain and congestion
reference.prognosis: Most patients respond rapidly to corticosteroids with resolution of pain and swelling, but relapses are frequent on tapering, and some develop chronic fibrosis with persistent restriction, proptosis, or visual loss; refractory cases may need steroid-sparing immunosuppression or radiotherapy.
pitfalls: Labelling an orbital mass idiopathic without excluding lymphoma and specific inflammations by biopsy
Mistaking it for orbital cellulitis and giving antibiotics alone, or vice versa
Attributing a poor steroid response to inadequate dosing rather than an alternative diagnosis
Overlooking IgG4-related disease and systemic vasculitis as underlying causes
Missing apical involvement threatening the optic nerve
management: Use systemic corticosteroids as first-line therapy, which typically produce a rapid, dramatic response supporting the diagnosis
Add steroid-sparing immunosuppression (methotrexate, mycophenolate) or rituximab for frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent disease
Reserve low-dose orbital radiotherapy for refractory cases
Treat urgently when apical involvement threatens the optic nerve
Perform orbital biopsy in atypical, bilateral, recurrent or steroid-unresponsive disease to exclude lymphoma and other mimics
Monitor closely for relapse during and after corticosteroid tapering
Manage under an orbital and ophthalmology specialist, with systemic evaluation for sarcoidosis, vasculitis or IgG4-related disease
